title: Securitize Counters Anti-Tokenization WSJ Ad With Full-Page Response
description: Securitize answered a nonprofit's Wall Street Journal warning with its own full-page ad promoting one-for-one-backed, regulated tokenized shares.
why_it_matters: The competing ads expose a practical issuer-education battle: venue-specific third-party tokens, synthetic trackers and regulated security entitlements carry different rights and oversight.
keyTakeaways: The Common Sense Leadership Fund used an October 24-25 Wall Street Journal ad to urge public-company CEOs to resist third-party stock tokenization.
Securitize responded on October 28 with a full-page ad presenting one-for-one backing, shareholder rights and verified investors as its regulated model.
The SEC exemption is temporary and conditional; its issuer objection process applies after a venue gives written notice for a third-party token.
body:
A policy fight over tokenized stocks moved into paid newspaper advertising. CoinDesk reported that the Common Sense Leadership Fund placed a full-page warning in The Wall Street Journal's October 24-25 weekend edition. The ad addressed public-company CEOs, described third-party tokenization as a threat and urged them to act. CoinDesk said the nonprofit's ultimate campaign financing was not disclosed.

Securitize answered with its own full-page Journal ad on October 28. The company presented a different model: tokens backed one-for-one by actual shares, carrying voting and dividend rights, offered through an SEC-registered broker-dealer to verified investors. Those are Securitize's claims about its structure, not a blanket description of every tokenized stock product.

The regulatory distinction matters. The SEC's September 17 order is temporary and conditional. For stock tokenized by an unaffiliated third party, a covered venue must provide the issuer written notice and an opportunity to object. CoinDesk also reported that the first ad linked to a Nasdaq FAQ, while Nasdaq denied involvement with the campaign. The advertising exchange is a new event, separate from the previously reported OKXICE issuer objections, and does not establish that either ad caused any issuer decision.

facts.claim: The nonprofit advertisement addressed public-company chief executives and framed third-party tokens as their problem.
facts.anchor: YOUR STOCK. THEIR TOKENS. YOUR PROBLEM.

facts.claim: CoinDesk identified the sponsor as the Common Sense Leadership Fund and said its ultimate campaign financing remained unclear.
facts.anchor: Who ultimately financed the campaign remains unclear

facts.claim: Securitize's October 28 response said tokenization done correctly should follow Wall Street rules.
facts.anchor: TOKENIZATION DONE RIGHT PLAYS BY THEM

facts.claim: The Securitize advertisement described its model as backed one-for-one by real shares with voting and dividend rights.
Nasdaq told CoinDesk it had no connection to the nonprofit advertisement or its use of Nasdaq's FAQ.
facts.anchor: had no connection to the advertisement

facts.claim: The SEC characterized its tokenized-stock venue relief as temporary and conditional.
Covered venues must give issuers written notice and an opportunity to object before third-party tokenized stock trading.
